category: Basics, classification, and language about autism
definition_en: Autism, or autism spectrum disorder (ASD), is a neurodevelopmental condition in which characteristics of social communication and interaction are combined with restricted or repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or sensory responses. Presentation and support needs vary widely and may change throughout life. Diagnosis is made by a professional based on a developmental history and a comprehensive assessment, not a single blood test or questionnaire.
where_encountered_en: A report from a psychiatrist or other authorized professional, developmental consultation, school recommendations, and parenting resources.
example_en: The report says "ASD": this is the name of a diagnostic category, but it alone does not indicate how a child communicates, learns, or what support preferences.
dont_confuse_en: ASD is not the same as intellectual disability, lack of verbal language, or a specific level of independence, these characteristics are assessed separately.
parent_takeaway_en: Ask the specialist not only for the diagnosis, but also for a description of strengths, needs, support goals, and next steps.

category: Basics, classification, and language about autism
definition_en: Neurodiversity is a concept that describes the natural variety in the ways in which human nervous systems are structured and function. It is used to discuss differences in perception, attention, communication, and learning without automatically framing any difference as a deficit. Neurodiversity refers to the variety of people in a group or society, an individual is more often described as neurodivergent or neurotypical.
where_encountered_en: Discussions of inclusion, educational accommodations, human rights, professional and public publications.
example_en: A school talks about "classroom neurodiversity," acknowledging that students may respond to different ways of explaining and completing a task.
dont_confuse_en: Neurodiversity is not a medical diagnosis and is not a reason to refuse treatment for underlying conditions or necessary support.
parent_takeaway_en: Consider what specific conditions help your child participate in school and everyday life, a general term does not replace a needs assessment.

category: Basics, classification, and language about autism
definition_en: The autism spectrum refers to a wide range of combinations of autistic characteristics and needs, not a single straight line from "mild" to "severe." One person may have advanced skills in one area and significant difficulties in another. Needs also depend on the context: the environment, access to communication, health status, and the demands of the situation.
where_encountered_en: Explaining the ASD diagnosis, discussing adaptations and the level of support needed.
example_en: A child reads well, but has difficulty maintaining a noisy school hallway and explaining when a break is needed. This is not a contradiction, but an example of an uneven profile.
dont_confuse_en: "Spectrum" is not an IQ score, a linear ability rating, or an unchangeable life prognosis.
parent_takeaway_en: Clarify the profile separately for communication, sensory needs, daily living skills, and support in different settings.

term_en: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision
category: Basics, classification, and language about autism
definition_en: The DSM-5-TR is the fifth revised edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, published by the American Psychiatric Association in 2022. It presents diagnostic criteria and explanations, including for ASD. It is a professional guide to classification and assessment, not a test that parents can take on their own to establish a diagnosis.
where_encountered_en: A psychiatric or psychological report, discussion of diagnostic criteria, and research.
example_en: The specialist states that they took into account the DSM-5-TR criteria and the child's developmental history during the assessment.
dont_confuse_en: The DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 are different classification systems, the presence of a criterion in the DSM does not automatically mean that the American rules for making a diagnosis are applied in Kazakhstan.
parent_takeaway_en: You can ask the specialist to explain which observations meet the criteria and what other reasons were considered.

category: Basics, classification, and language about autism
definition_en: ICD-11 is the eleventh revision of the World Health Organization's International Classification of Diseases. It contains international diagnostic categories and codes, autism spectrum disorder belongs to group 6A02, which is specified for intellectual development and functional language. The international entry into force of ICD-11 does not equate to the completion of its implementation in all national systems. In Kazakhstan, the transition to ICD-11 is provided for in strategic planning documents, the version of the classification for a specific medical document should be clarified with the healthcare organization.
where_encountered_en: Medical reports, electronic diagnosis records, professional guidelines, and scientific publications.
example_en: The physician explains how the description of the condition relates to category 6A02 of ICD-11, but the official code in the local system may depend on the version of the classification used.
dont_confuse_en: ICD-11 is not a test for autism, Do not independently replace the code in the ICD-10 document with the ICD-11 code. DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 cannot be mechanically equated.
parent_takeaway_en: If documents contain different codes, check with the issuing organization to determine which classification is officially used and how the entry is interpreted.

category: Basics, classification, and language about autism
definition_en: Differential diagnosis is the sequential comparison of several possible explanations for observed characteristics and symptoms. If ASD is suspected, the specialist considers, for example, language difficulties, hearing impairments, intellectual developmental issues, anxiety, and other causes, some conditions may coexist with autism.
where_encountered_en: Diagnostic consultation, conclusion of the interdisciplinary team, referrals for additional examinations.
example_en: If the child does not respond to being addressed by name, the specialist determines not only the child's social attention characteristics but also their hearing status.
dont_confuse_en: Differential diagnosis does not mean the specialist denies the observed difficulties or that all the listed conditions are mutually exclusive.
parent_takeaway_en: Ask which possible causes have already been assessed, which still need to be assessed, and how the results will change the support plan.

category: Basics, classification, and language about autism
definition_en: Comorbidity, or co-occurring conditions, is the presence of two or more medical, psychiatric, or neurodevelopmental conditions in one person. For example, an autistic child may also have ADHD, epilepsy, anxiety disorder, or sleep disorders. Each co-occurring condition requires its own assessment and, if necessary, intervention.
where_encountered_en: Medical history, doctor consultation, support plan, results of an interdisciplinary assessment.
example_en: A child is diagnosed with ASD, and later a doctor diagnoses epilepsy. The second diagnosis does not cancel the first, but requires separate medical monitoring.
dont_confuse_en: Do not automatically attribute any pain, sleep disturbances, seizures, or behavioral changes to autism. They may have another cause.
parent_takeaway_en: Report new symptoms to a specialist even after ASD is diagnosed, Ask to evaluate complaints and not attribute them to the underlying diagnosis.

category: Basics, classification, and language about autism
definition_en: Developmental regression is a noticeable loss of skills that a child previously mastered reliably, such as previously used words, gestures, social or motor skills. It is a description of a developmental change, not a stand-alone diagnosis. Loss of skills requires evaluation by a specialist, as possible causes vary and are not limited to autism.
where_encountered_en: Early developmental interview, medical history, and speech and motor assessment.
example_en: A child used familiar words regularly for several months but then stopped using them and no longer uses them in familiar situations.
dont_confuse_en: Regression is not the same as a short-term refusal to speak in unfamiliar situations, fluctuations in performance, or a lack of progress. Loss of motor skills or sudden, significant changes require prompt medical evaluation.
parent_takeaway_en: Record which skills specifically disappeared, when, and under what circumstances, and discuss this with your pediatrician, do not wait for a routine checkup if there is sudden or progressive skill loss.

category: Basics, classification, and language about autism
definition_en: Autistic camouflage, or disguise, is a strategy a person uses to hide or compensate for autistic traits that are noticeable to others. This may include consciously copying gestures, preparing phrases for communication, or restraining habitual movements. Such adaptations sometimes help cope with social demands, but can require significant effort.
where_encountered_en: Discussion of late diagnosis, school adaptation, social fatigue, and psychological consultation.
example_en: At school, a teenager rehearses answers in advance and tries to appear calm, but after the school day feels very exhausted.
dont_confuse_en: Disguise alone does not confirm a diagnosis and should not automatically explain any difficulties, the absence of noticeable external manifestations also does not rule out autism.
parent_takeaway_en: When describing everyday difficulties, consider not only the visible behavior in the reception, but also the cost of effort, fatigue, and differences between situations.

definition_en: Receptive language is the ability to understand language messages: spoken and, with appropriate experience, written or signed speech, words, sentences, and their meaning in context. Understanding language may differ from the ability to pronounce words or express thoughts. When assessing, a specialist takes into account the child's age, language environment, hearing, available channels of information presentation, and response methods.
where_encountered_en: Speech therapy report, language and communication assessment, educational support program.
example_en: The child cannot name an object out loud, but correctly selects it from several pictures when verbally requested, this helps assess comprehension separately from pronunciation.
dont_confuse_en: Good comprehension of individual instructions does not indicate equal comprehension of longer explanations, lack of response does not always indicate lack of understanding.
parent_takeaway_en: Ask to assess understanding and expression of language separately and to use the child's available response methods.

definition_en: Expressive language is the ability to express the content of a message using language: words and sentences, writing, sign language, and, when necessary, AAC. Assessment considers not only the number of words spoken, but also the meanings a person can convey, the variety of messages, and whether appropriate modes of expression are available. Expressive language development and comprehension of spoken language do not always coincide.
where_encountered_en: Speech therapy report, communication assessment, individual educational and therapeutic goals.
example_en: The child understands the question "What do you want?" but cannot pronounce the answer, s/he selects the "water" symbol on the communicator.
dont_confuse_en: Expressive language is not the same as articulation: clarity of pronunciation and the ability to formulate thoughts are different areas. The absence of spoken language does not prove a lack of thought or linguistic comprehension.
parent_takeaway_en: Ask a specialist to evaluate speech, comprehension, and available alternative communication methods separately. It's important to assess whether the child can request, refuse, comment, and seek help.

definition_en: Pragmatics of language is how a person understands and uses language in a specific social situation. This includes the intent of the statement, the order of responses, the choice of words that are understandable to the interlocutor, clarifying questions, understanding of context and indirect meaning. Communication norms depend on the culture and language environment, there is no single obligatory style of conversational behavior.
where_encountered_en: Speech therapy assessment of social communication, school characteristics, recommendations of a communication specialist.
example_en: A teenager explains a favorite topic in detail, but it is difficult for him to notice that the interlocutor does not know the background, the specialist suggests ways to clarify the context.
dont_confuse_en: Pragmatics is not synonymous with friendliness, good manners, or a "desire to communicate." A direct style of speech or unusual eye contact are not in themselves a diagnosis.
parent_takeaway_en: Discuss the practical goal: how to make communication mutually understandable without requiring imitation of social gestures at the cost of expressed discomfort.

search_aliases: CAS; speech apraxia; детская апраксия речи
definition_en: Childhood apraxia of speech (CAS) is a neurological disorder of planning and programming the movements needed to produce sounds and their sequences, muscle weakness is not a necessary cause. Inconsistent errors in repeating a single word, difficulty transitioning between syllables, and atypical stress may occur. No single symptom alone confirms CAS, a comprehensive motor-speech assessment is required.
where_encountered_en: An evaluation by a speech therapist specializing in motor speech disorders reveals severe sound production difficulties.
example_en: The child attempts to pronounce the same word several times, but the sound composition changes each time, the specialist tests repeated tasks of varying difficulty.
dont_confuse_en: CAS cannot be diagnosed solely because a child does not speak, has ASD, or produces few words. Apraxia differs from dysarthria, phonological disorder, and language disorder.
parent_takeaway_en: Ask for clarification on the signs that support the hypothesis, how changes will be measured, and what AAC methods will allow the child to communicate during oral speech development.

definition_en: Echolalia is the repetition of previously heard words, phrases, or other linguistic sequences. The repetition may occur shortly after another person speaks or after a long period of time. Echolalia has various functions: request, participation in a conversation, confirmation, self-regulation, or repetition whose communicative function has not yet been established. The meaning is determined by the context, not just the form of the phrase.
where_encountered_en: Conversation with a speech therapist, communication assessment, description of the child's spontaneous speech.
example_en: A child says a phrase from a cartoon when asking to turn on their favorite show, the adult notes in which situations the phrase appears.
dont_confuse_en: Echolalia is not necessarily "meaningless repetition" and does not prove the existence of the GLP model or the need for the NLA protocol. It's impossible to conclude from a single repeated phrase whether a child understood it or not.
parent_takeaway_en: Record not only the phrase itself, but also the situation, who it was addressed to, and what happened afterward. Ask the specialist to maintain and expand on existing communication methods.

search_aliases: АДК; AAC; альтернативная коммуникация; дополнительная коммуникация
definition_en: Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) are ways to support or replace spoken language when a person has difficulty conveying or understanding messages in a commonly available way. AAC includes gestures, signs, symbols, communication boards, written words, apps, and devices with speech output. "Augmentative" communication complements speech, while "alternative" communication can replace it. An AAC system should support the expression of a person's own messages. With motor assistance, it is important to ensure that the user, and not the assistant, selects the message content.
where_encountered_en: Speech therapy assessment, individual support program, school, communicator selection.
example_en: The child selects "I need a break" on the tablet and hears the voiced message, adults honor the request.
dont_confuse_en: AAC is a broad area of ​​communication support, and PECS is a distinct technique within it. Regular communicators and independent symbol pointing should not be confused with FC, RPM, or S2C, for which professional organizations cite issues with proving independent authorship of messages and dependency on the facilitator.
parent_takeaway_en: Ask for access to communication for requests, refusals, choices, comments, and interactions, not just for responding to tasks. Partner training in communication and constant accessibility are essential.

definition_en: PECS (Picture Exchange Communication System) is a specific, structured system for teaching functional communication through the exchange of pictures. It includes six sequential phases: from person-initiated exchange of a single picture to picture discrimination, sentence construction, and responding to questions and comments. PECS is one approach within AAC, not all picture communication is PECS. The choice of method should take into account individual needs and available alternatives.
where_encountered_en: Speech-language pathology program, requesting and social communication training methods, and an individualized support plan.
example_en: The child brings a picture of a "ball" to an adult to request a play, rather than waiting for lengthy verbal instructions.
dont_confuse_en: Not every flashcard or visual schedule is PECS, PECS is not the same as all AAC. Don't promise that following these steps will automatically produce spoken language or will be optimal for every child.
parent_takeaway_en: Discuss whether the approach encourages independent initiative, whether refusal and other meanings can be expressed, and whether more appropriate forms of AAC are available.

definition_en: Joint attention is the coordination of two people's attention toward a single object, action, or event with the understanding that attention is shared. This can be demonstrated through gaze, pointing, showing an object, words, or an accessible AAC method. Forms of joint attention depend on the individual's motor, sensory, and communicative abilities.
where_encountered_en: Early social communication assessment, play support program, specialist opinion.
example_en: A child notices an unusual bird, points to it, and turns to an adult to share their interest, not just to get the object.
dont_confuse_en: Joint attention does not require constant eye contact. Asking for an object and sharing interest are related but different communicative actions.
parent_takeaway_en: Ask how the specialist will notice and support the child's initiatives through accessible methods of communication and events of interest to him.

definition_en: Social reciprocity is the mutual influence and response of participants in communication: one person suggests a topic, action, or signal, the other responds, and the exchange continues. Reciprocity can occur in conversation, play, sign language, written language, or AAC communication. Its manifestations depend on the context, cultural norms, relationship with the interlocutor, and individual communication style.
where_encountered_en: Diagnostic discussion of social skills, speech therapy assessment, recommendations for joint play.
example_en: Two children take turns adding pieces to a shared structure and showing each other the results - this is one type of reciprocal interaction.
dont_confuse_en: Social reciprocity is not the same as obedience or talkativeness. An unusual communication style does not indicate that a person is not interested in a relationship.
parent_takeaway_en: Ask to describe specific interactions in a safe and familiar environment, rather than judging the child based on a formal “normative” conversation style.

definition_en: Sensory processing is the process by which the nervous system receives, distinguishes, and uses information from the senses and internal receptors. This includes the processing of sound, light, touch, taste, movement, body position, and internal cues. People have different response profiles: some stimuli may be perceived as too intense, others as not noticeable enough.
where_encountered_en: Occupational therapist assessment, discussion about daily difficulties, school environmental recommendations.
example_en: Child covers ears in noisy cafeteria but plays calmly in a quiet room, specific conditions are important for support.
dont_confuse_en: Sensory differences are not the same as a diagnosis of ASD on their own and do not mean that every sensory intervention is necessary or scientifically proven.
parent_takeaway_en: Note specific stimuli and the impact on the child's participation, Discuss the adaptation of space and tasks with a specialist.

definition_en: Sensory hyperreactivity is an increased or intense response to certain sensory stimuli relative to their usual intensity. Sound, light, touch, or odor may cause marked discomfort, avoidance, or difficulty continuing an activity. The response may depend on the individual's condition, previous stress, and environment, it does not necessarily manifest itself in all sensory systems.
where_encountered_en: Sensory profile, complaints about noise, bright lighting, clothing, and grooming procedures.
example_en: A child has difficulty putting on a T-shirt with a stiff tag, although seamless clothing does not interfere.
dont_confuse_en: Hyperreactivity does not mean "capriciousness" and is not the same as complete intolerance of any sensations. One reaction does not confirm the diagnosis.
parent_takeaway_en: Find out which properties of the stimulus are causing difficulty, and together with your child, choose acceptable changes without forcing them to get used to the pain.

definition_en: Sensory hyporeactivity is a weak, delayed, or less noticeable response to certain sensory stimuli. A person may be late in noticing handling, touch, or other changes in the environment, the pattern varies across different senses and situations. A description of the sensory profile does not replace medical exclusion of hearing, vision, or other causes.
where_encountered_en: Occupational therapist assessment, observation of response to sounds, touch, and environmental changes.
example_en: A child may not notice that clothes are wet, but react strongly to a loud siren: both phenomena can coexist.
dont_confuse_en: Lack of response to name does not prove hyporeactivity and does not exclude hearing impairment. Hyporeactivity does not mean that a child "does not feel anything."
parent_takeaway_en: If you have persistent suspicions, notify your doctor, compare reactions in different circumstances and consider safety.

definition_en: Sensory seeking is a behavior in which a person actively seeks out certain sensations, such as rocking, pressure on the body, rhythmic sounds, or movement. This behavior may help maintain alertness, experience pleasurable sensations, or regulate state. The specific function is determined by observation, not just the appearance of the action.
where_encountered_en: Sensory profile, occupational therapist recommendations, observations at home and school.
example_en: The child enjoys jumping up and down after sitting for a long time, the specialist checks if an accessible and safe break helps return to activity.
dont_confuse_en: Sensory seeking is not the same as hyporeactivity and is not always a "bad habit." Not every repetitive movement has a purely sensory cause.
parent_takeaway_en: First, assess whether the action is safe and whether it interferes with important activities, Look for ways to provide the desired feeling without being too restrictive.

definition_en: Sensory overload is a colloquial description of a condition in which the sum or intensity of sensory information exceeds a person's current ability to tolerate and process it. Overload may be accompanied by fatigue, irritation, a desire to withdraw, decreased speech, or a strong emotional reaction. This is a condition, not a separate medical diagnostic category.
where_encountered_en: Discussion of school difficulties, crowded public places, load management, and environmental adaptation.
example_en: After a noisy holiday, the child stops answering questions and wants to go to a quiet room.
dont_confuse_en: Do not attribute any sudden change in behavior to "sensory overload": pain, illness, hunger, anxiety, or a seizure require separate consideration.
parent_takeaway_en: Provide voluntary exit to a quiet place, reduction of stimuli, and communication without additional demands, If you experience any unusual or acute symptoms, seek medical attention.

definition_en: Proprioception is the sense of position, movement, and force of body parts, generated by signals from muscles, tendons, and joints. It helps children navigate without constantly monitoring their eyes, plan the force of movement, maintain posture, and coordinate actions. Proprioception interacts with vision, the vestibular, and other sensory systems.
where_encountered_en: Occupational therapy, coordination assessment, motor tasks, discussion of movement needs.
example_en: A child learns to lift a cup with the right amount of force without squeezing too hard or spilling the water.
dont_confuse_en: Proprioception is not the same as general physical strength and is not a standalone test for autism, motor difficulties can have various causes.
parent_takeaway_en: If movements interfere with daily tasks or safety, discuss assessing motor and sensory factors instead of generic "proprioception" exercises.

definition_en: Interoception is the perception and interpretation of signals from within the body, such as hunger, thirst, bladder fullness, heartbeat, and some sensations of discomfort. These signals help notice physical needs, but awareness and verbal description can vary significantly. The relationship of interoception to emotions is being studied, but behavior alone cannot reliably determine what a person is feeling.
where_encountered_en: Assess independence, discuss feeding, toilet skills, and recognition of bodily sensations.
example_en: The child has difficulty noticing the need to go to the toilet in advance, but is good at distinguishing food tastes.
dont_confuse_en: Difficulties with interoception should not be considered an explanation for all feeding problems or pain and do not replace a medical assessment of symptoms.
parent_takeaway_en: Use clear body cues and accessible reminders, while remaining respectful of the child's sensations, Discuss sudden changes with your doctor.

definition_en: Sensory integration is the processing and integration of information from different sensory systems for orientation, movement, and everyday activities. The term describes neurophysiological processes and is also used in the names of therapeutic models. Integrating different signals occurs in all people, the presence of sensory difficulties alone does not confirm the need for a specific type of therapy.
where_encountered_en: Occupational therapist work, assessment of sensory processing and coordination, description of the therapeutic program.
example_en: To catch a ball, a child integrates visual information, a sense of hand position, and information about body movement.
dont_confuse_en: The process of sensory integration is not identical to the Ayres Sensory Integration (ASI) method. Promises of a universal effect from "sensory integration" are scientifically unfounded.
parent_takeaway_en: Ask for a specific goal, the results of the initial assessment, the approach chosen, and how progress will be measured in everyday life.

definition_en: Stimming is a common term for repetitive movements, sounds, or other actions that can provide pleasant sensations, help with focus, express emotions, or regulate tension. Examples include rocking, repeating a sound, or fiddling with an object. These actions are not unique to autistic people, their function and meaning vary from person to person.
where_encountered_en: Discussion about behavioral characteristics, sensory regulation, school adaptations, and participation in activities.
example_en: Rocking in a chair while waiting helps the child remain calm.
dont_confuse_en: Stimming is not automatically dangerous and does not require suppression just because it is unusual. If there is a risk of self-harm, an assessment of the cause and safe alternatives are necessary.
parent_takeaway_en: Discuss whether the action is harmful to the child or to safety, not just to others, maintain safe methods of self-regulation.

definition_en: Stereotypies are a clinical descriptive term for relatively repetitive, similarly shaped movements, postures, sounds, or actions. They can occur in a variety of situations, have different functions, and are found in autism, other conditions, and typical development. Form, onset, duration, contextual relevance, and impact on daily functioning are important for assessment.
where_encountered_en: Neurological or psychiatric description, behavioral assessment, observational recording.
example_en: A professional describes "stereotypic hand movements" when a child repeatedly makes a similar movement when joyful.
dont_confuse_en: Stereotypy is a characteristic of an action, not necessarily a diagnosis. It must be distinguished from tics, seizures, compulsions, and involuntary movement disorders, especially when they have an unusual onset.
parent_takeaway_en: If you notice any new or suspicious movements, describe them to a specialist and, if possible, record a video, do not suppress safe actions based on appearance alone.

definition_en: Cognitive rigidity is difficulty changing a way of thinking, a habitual plan, a rule, or a strategy when circumstances change. It may manifest as a strong need for predictability or difficulty transitioning to a new task. Severity depends on fatigue, anxiety, sensory overload, clarity of instructions, and available support.
where_encountered_en: Psychological assessment, discussion of transitions between lessons and changes in routine.
example_en: When a lesson is unexpectedly canceled, the child has difficulty switching to another activity, even if they usually enjoy it.
dont_confuse_en: Rigidity is not the same as stubbornness or malicious resistance and does not, in itself, confirm ASD. Cognitive flexibility is a related executive function, not a moral characteristic.
parent_takeaway_en: Offer change alerts, visual plans, and a choice of options, ask what environmental changes reduce the load.

definition_en: Meltdown is an informal term for a severe reaction of distress or overwhelm that makes it extremely difficult for a person to maintain normal control over behavior and communication. It may be accompanied by crying, screaming, motor agitation, or an attempt to escape. It is not a separate diagnosis, the causes can be sensory, emotional, medical, or situational.
where_encountered_en: Conversations between the family and a psychologist, a description of severe distress at school, a prevention and safety plan.
example_en: After a combination of loud noises, a long wait, and a sudden change in schedule, the child cries and tries to leave the room.
dont_confuse_en: It is impossible to reliably distinguish meltdown from pain, a panic reaction, or another condition based on the external reaction. What is happening should not be automatically interpreted as an attempt to achieve a desired goal.
parent_takeaway_en: During an episode, first ensure safety and reduce demands and stimuli, later, when calm, address possible triggers. If unusual or acute symptoms occur, seek medical attention.

definition_en: Shutdown is an informal description of a state of markedly reduced activity, initiative, or communication in response to intense stress. A person may become silent, reduce movement, isolate themselves from what is happening, or require solitude. This is not an official clinical diagnosis, but a description of an observed condition, the causes of which should be clarified.
where_encountered_en: Discussion of overload at school, after trips, social events, or intense activities.
example_en: After a difficult day, a teenager has difficulty answering even simple questions, they choose a quiet room and temporarily communicate with short messages.
dont_confuse_en: Shutdown should not be used as a universal explanation for sudden immobility, loss of consciousness, severe drowsiness, or unresponsiveness. Such symptoms may require urgent medical evaluation.
parent_takeaway_en: Provide a calm environment, time to recover, and an alternative channel of communication. If the condition is new, sudden, or accompanied by alarming symptoms, seek medical attention.

definition_en: Alexithymia is the difficulty recognizing, distinguishing, and describing one's own emotional states. A person may feel tension in the body but not understand whether it is related to fear, anger, fatigue, or another emotion. Alexithymia is studied as a psychological characteristic and can be combined with various conditions, it is not a mandatory sign of autism.
where_encountered_en: Consultation with a psychologist, discussion of emotions, self-regulation, and the connection between sensations and emotional experience.
example_en: A teenager says, "I feel bad," but cannot clarify the emotional state, a specialist helps distinguish between bodily signals and context.
dont_confuse_en: Alexithymia does not mean a lack of emotions, empathy, or concern for others. You cannot infer a person's experiences solely by how easily they name them.
parent_takeaway_en: Use a variety of ways to describe the condition: words, scales, pictures, or text, avoid forcing an immediate verbal response.

definition_en: Executive functions are a group of cognitive processes that enable you to maintain a goal, plan steps, control impulses, shift attention, use working memory, and change strategy. They are needed not only for learning but also for everyday activities such as getting ready, sequencing tasks, and time management. The executive function profile can be uneven.
where_encountered_en: Psychological and neuropsychological assessment, school recommendations, difficulties with organization.
example_en: The child knows the order of morning activities, but without a visual list, often skips one of the steps.
dont_confuse_en: Executive difficulties are not a measure of intelligence or diligence. They occur in various conditions and do not establish a diagnosis of ASD or ADHD.
parent_takeaway_en: Break down complex tasks into manageable steps, use external reminders, and ask for feedback on which component of the task is the most challenging.

definition_en: Global Developmental Delay (GDD) is a clinical designation for significant delay in two or more developmental areas in a young child, usually under five years of age. Examples of skills assessed include motor, language, cognitive, and social skills. It is a description of a developmental profile that requires investigation of possible causes, it does not automatically indicate autism or intellectual disability.
where_encountered_en: A pediatrician, pediatric neurologist, early intervention service, and developmental assessment report.
example_en: A three-year-old child exhibits simultaneous difficulties with sentence construction and motor skill acquisition, the specialist is discussing the need for a more comprehensive assessment.
dont_confuse_en: GDD is a descriptive clinical category for delays in multiple developmental areas in a young child. It is not equivalent to ASD, does not prove intellectual disability, and does not predict future development based on a single assessment, causes and dynamics must be assessed separately.
parent_takeaway_en: Ask for a description of the specific areas assessed, what the current support goals are, and whether further testing of vision, hearing, neurological, or genetic conditions is needed.

term_en: Disorder of intellectual development / Intellectual disability (ID)
definition_en: Intellectual disability (ID) is a condition characterized by significant limitations in intellectual functioning and adaptive behavior that arise during development. Assessment focuses on learning, reasoning, and problem-solving abilities, as well as real-world conceptual, social, and practical skills in everyday life. The assessment should consider language, culture, sensory, and motor limitations.
where_encountered_en: Clinical and psychological assessment, assessment of adaptive skills, discussion of necessary daily supports.
example_en: The specialist compares not only the intelligence test result but also the person's ability to perform everyday activities in an accessible environment.
dont_confuse_en: Intellectual disability is not the same as ASD, lack of speech, or a low score on one test. The formulations and criteria in the DSM, ICD, and AAIDD have specific characteristics that should not be mechanically mixed.
parent_takeaway_en: Clarify which tools were used, whether accessible communication methods were used, and how the findings relate to specific types of support.

definition_en: Adaptive functioning is how well a person typically applies acquired skills to participate in everyday life, taking into account age and context. Typically, conceptual (language, money, time), social (interaction, safety, social understanding), and practical (self-care, routine, everyday activities) domains are considered. Actual task performance should be assessed, not just potential ability in a test situation.
where_encountered_en: Psychological assessment, adaptive behavior questionnaires, educational plan, discussion of independence.
example_en: A child can tie shoelaces in class, but in the morning rush regularly needs prompting - this is important for assessing functioning in context.
dont_confuse_en: Adaptive functioning is not the same as IQ and does not mean that a person should do everything without support. Abilities can vary greatly across areas and situations.
parent_takeaway_en: Ask to identify specific skills, the conditions under which they are achieved, and what tools, assistance, and training actually enhance independence.

definition_en: Adaptive skills are individual, mastered actions that help a person cope with life's tasks: communicating a need, dressing, following a schedule, moving safely, managing simple purchases, maintaining personal hygiene. They are components of the broader concept of adaptive functioning. The level of skills depends on age, abilities, education, and the accessibility of the environment.
where_encountered_en: School and individual support programs, assessment of everyday independence and social adaptation.
example_en: The goal of "independently communicating the need for a break" is a specific adaptive skill that can be learned verbally, by gesture, or through AAC.
dont_confuse_en: An adaptive skill is not limited to obedience or performing a task only on command from an adult. Not every everyday skill is appropriate for every child at the same age.
parent_takeaway_en: Formulate practical goals: what a person wants or needs to be able to do, what conditions and prompts are needed, how to check the transfer to everyday life.

definition_en: Screening is a preliminary examination using a standardized tool that helps identify an increased likelihood of developmental disabilities or the need for an in-depth examination. Unlike ongoing developmental monitoring, screening is conducted using a specific procedure, questionnaire, or set of tasks. The result does not establish a diagnosis and does not replace a full clinical assessment, a positive result requires further action.
where_encountered_en: A preventive visit to a pediatrician, questionnaire, developmental assessment at a children's clinic.
example_en: The questionnaire indicates an increased likelihood of developmental disabilities, and the doctor offers a full diagnostic assessment.
dont_confuse_en: A positive screening result does not mean "autism is confirmed," and a negative screening result does not guarantee a complete absence of difficulties, especially if there are observable warning signs.
parent_takeaway_en: Report specific observations to the doctor regardless of the questionnaire score, Find out what to do next and whether a re-evaluation is needed.

term_en: Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers, Revised, with Follow-Up
search_aliases: MCHAT; M-CHAT; M CHAT R F
definition_en: M-CHAT-R/F is a standardized two-stage screening tool for children aged 16-30 months, aimed at identifying an increased likelihood of autism. After the initial M-CHAT-R, with a total score of 3-7, a special follow-up interview is conducted only on risk points. With a score of 8-20, a follow-up is not required: referral for a diagnostic evaluation and early intervention is recommended. With a score of 0-2, the screening is usually negative, but this does not cancel the assessment if parents or specialists still have concerns. Screening scores are not a diagnosis.
where_encountered_en: Initial consultation with a pediatrician, early development screening program, referral for additional testing.
example_en: After the initial questionnaire, a result is obtained that requires a follow-up interview. The specialist asks additional questions about the child's behavior in ordinary situations.
dont_confuse_en: Follow-Up is a separate structured interview, not a re-administered questionnaire. Unintelligible translations are not permitted, nor are scores interpreted as diagnostic. Use and reproduction of the full instrument are governed by the copyright holder's terms and conditions, particularly in electronic products.
parent_takeaway_en: Please clarify whether the age-appropriate version was used, whether the Follow-Up phase was conducted according to the algorithm, and where to address any persistent developmental issues.

term_en: Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule, Second Edition
search_aliases: ADOS; АДОС; Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule
definition_en: The ADOS-2 (Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule, Second Edition) is a standardized, semi-structured clinical observation instrument for measuring social communication, interaction, play, and limited repetitive behavior in structured settings. It contains five modules, including a module for young children, the appropriate module is selected based on age and expressive language level. Results are assessed by a trained professional along with developmental history and other data. The ADOS-2 alone does not establish or exclude a diagnosis of ASD.
where_encountered_en: Comprehensive ASD diagnostic assessment, a report by a specialized team, and a description of the standardized assessment results.
example_en: The professional conducts play or conversation tasks and compares observations with data from parents, teachers, and a medical history.
dont_confuse_en: The ADOS-2 should not be considered a blood test, a standalone "autism detector," or a sufficient sole basis for a diagnosis. The final score does not automatically reflect all actual support needs.
parent_takeaway_en: Ask for clarification on the meaning of the results, the limitations of the method, and how they were compared with data outside the office.

search_aliases: ABA; АВА; ПАП; прикладной анализ поведения
definition_en: Applied behavior analysis (ABA) is a field of behavioral science and practical methods that uses the observation of relationships between environmental conditions, actions, and their consequences to achieve learning and behavior change. Autism programs employ a variety of formats, from structured instruction to everyday situations. Program quality depends on goals, the qualifications of the specialists, respect for individual autonomy, transparency of measurement, and the absence of harmful practices.
where_encountered_en: Behavior specialist program, skills training plan, discussion of the functional behavior assessment.
example_en: Instead of the goal of "sit quietly at any cost," the team chooses the goal: the child can independently request a break in an accessible way and use this skill at home and at school.
dont_confuse_en: ABA is a diverse field of methods, not a single therapy with proven results for everyone. Research findings from individual interventions should not be generalized to any program or declared harmless: a systematic review by Project AIM (2024) found insufficient monitoring and reporting of adverse effects. Suppressing safe stimming and ignoring refusal should not be standalone program goals.
parent_takeaway_en: Check which skills will actually improve quality of life, whether there are agreed-upon measurable goals, respect for refusal, protection from coercion, and regular assessment of benefits and adverse effects.

definition_en: Functional Behavior Assessment (FBA) is a systematic collection and analysis of information about behavior, the context in which it occurs, and possible causes and consequences. The team considers health status, pain, communication, task demands, and the sensory and social environment, not just the frequency of the behavior. The result is a testable hypothesis about why the behavior occurs or is maintained, and a plan to modify the conditions and teach accessible alternatives.
where_encountered_en: Developing a support plan for recurring dangerous or participation-interfering behavior.
example_en: A child pushes materials during a complex task. The team evaluates the complexity of the instruction, the need for a break, potential pain, and the ability to ask for help.
dont_confuse_en: FBA does not mean "find punishment," is not a psychiatric diagnosis, and is not reducible to the "attention-seeking behavior" paradigm. Functions can be combined and changed.
parent_takeaway_en: Ask to specify what data supports the hypothesis, how the plan reduces discomfort, and what available skills will be offered in lieu of risk or difficulty.

definition_en: Functional Communication Training (FCT) is an approach in which a person is taught an accessible way to communicate a need previously expressed through behavior that creates risk or difficulty. The communication method is selected after assessing the function of the behavior: it can be a word, a gesture, a card, or an AAC button. Key conditions are that the new signal must genuinely help obtain the necessary support and be within the person's capabilities.
where_encountered_en: A communication and behavior support plan, a collaborative effort between a speech-language pathologist, a behavioral specialist, and the family.
example_en: If a child drops objects when unable to complete a task, the team teaches them to clearly request "help" or "break" and consistently responds to this request.
dont_confuse_en: FCT is not limited to memorizing words: the child must have a real opportunity to communicate a need and receive a clear response. Some behavioral protocols include response extinction procedures, these are not a required feature of any FCT and require separate assessment of safety, consent, and the inadmissibility of coercion. This approach does not replace an assessment of pain, overload, or other medical causes.
parent_takeaway_en: Ask how the behavior's function has been confirmed, whether the child can initiate the signal independently, and how receptive others are to it.

definition_en: ADHD (Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder) is a neurodevelopmental disorder in which persistent patterns of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity significantly interfere with functioning in multiple life situations. Symptoms are assessed in the context of age, development, environment, and other possible explanations. ADHD can coexist with autism, and each condition requires a separate evaluation.
where_encountered_en: A report from a child psychiatrist, pediatrician, or other qualified professional, and school recommendations.
example_en: The child frequently loses track of actions and impulsively interrupts others at home and at school, the professional determines the duration of the behavior and its impact.
dont_confuse_en: ADHD does not equal bad manners, high activity, or "poor concentration" in one situation. A questionnaire alone is not enough for diagnosis.
parent_takeaway_en: Request a support plan with specific difficulties, environmental changes, school adaptations, and, if necessary, a separate clinical treatment assessment.

definition_en: Epilepsy is a brain disorder characterized by a persistent predisposition to epileptic seizures. Diagnosis is typically made after two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart, but according to ILAE criteria, it can also be established after a single unprovoked seizure with a sufficiently high risk of recurrence or in the presence of a known epileptic syndrome. Seizures are not always accompanied by convulsions: episodes of impaired awareness, freezing, and other manifestations are possible. The diagnosis is determined by a physician based on the clinical presentation and examination.
where_encountered_en: Consultation with a neurologist, EEG report, discussion of episodes of loss of contact or unusual movements.
example_en: The child briefly becomes unresponsive and stares into space, the physician determines the nature of the episode and the need for a neurological evaluation.
dont_confuse_en: Any "freezing" does not necessarily indicate epilepsy, but recurring episodes cannot be automatically attributed to autism. A normal EEG alone does not rule out epilepsy.
parent_takeaway_en: If you suspect a seizure, inform your doctor of the circumstances and duration, if possible, save the video. If the seizure is prolonged, breathing is impaired, or recurring seizures occur without recovery, seek emergency care immediately.

definition_en: ARFID (Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder) is a disorder of avoidant or restrictive food intake in which insufficient quantity or limited variety of food leads to significant eating or weight disturbances, dependence on supplements, or severe psychosocial difficulties. Possible mechanisms include sensory sensitivity, fear of unpleasant consequences of eating, and decreased interest in food. Unlike anorexia nervosa, the restriction is not motivated by fear of weight gain or a disturbed body image. Diagnosis requires the exclusion of alternative medical and other explanations.
where_encountered_en: Consultation with a pediatrician, gastroenterologist, clinical psychologist, and nutritionist in cases of severe food selectivity.
example_en: The child eats an extremely limited range of foods, resulting in nutrient deficiencies or serious eating difficulties at school.
dont_confuse_en: ARFID is not the same as typical age-related pickiness, and a normal weight does not rule out nutritional deficiencies. Swallowing problems, pain, allergies, gastrointestinal, and other medical causes should also be assessed.
parent_takeaway_en: Avoid coercion or punishment for food refusal, if weight loss, signs of dehydration, or growth disturbances occur, consult a doctor and discuss multidisciplinary care.

definition_en: PMPK is a psychological, medical and pedagogical consultation in the education system of Kazakhstan. In accordance with the Model Rules, it examines and consults children from birth to 18 years of age, determines special educational needs, recommended learning conditions and the type of educational program, and refers them for special psychological and pedagogical support. An appeal is possible at the initiative of the parents or by referral from an educational or medical organization with the consent of the parents. The result of the work is a conclusion and recommendations, the choice of educational organization is given to the parents.
where_encountered_en: Parents' application for an assessment of educational needs, preparation of recommendations for a kindergarten or school.
example_en: The family receives a PMPK conclusion with recommendations on special educational conditions and discusses their implementation with the educational organization.
dont_confuse_en: PMPK is not a VKK and does not establish disability instead of the ITU, Its conclusion does not replace a medical diagnosis of ASD. The PMPK recommendations and the clinical diagnosis serve different functions.
parent_takeaway_en: Parents can initiate an appeal and receive the PMPK's conclusion and recommendations in person. Clarify the recommended educational conditions and their implementation at the school, check current forms and registration procedures against current state regulations.

definition_en: The VKK is a medical advisory commission operating in a medical organization in Kazakhstan. According to the Regulation on the Activities of the VKK, its powers include, in particular, reviewing issues of referral for medical and social expertise, temporary disability assessment, certain types of medical care, and medical grounds for homeschooling a child. Conclusions are issued according to established medical forms, the VKK does not independently determine disability.
where_encountered_en: Outpatient clinic, referral to the MSE, preparation of medical reports, discussion of the need for additional types of assistance.
example_en: After examinations, the attending physician sends documents for review by the VKK, which evaluates the validity of referring the patient to the MSE.
dont_confuse_en: The VKK is not the same as the PMPK. The VKK does not replace the medical and social expertise itself and does not guarantee the determination of disability. A medical opinion from the VKK is not equivalent to an educational report.
parent_takeaway_en: Check with your treating physician to determine the specific decision required from the VKK, what materials are needed, and what document will be issued.

term_en: Medical and social assessment / expertise (Kazakhstan MSE)
definition_en: MSE is a medical and social examination conducted in Kazakhstan by authorized territorial divisions of the social protection system. In accordance with established procedures, it assesses persistent impairments of bodily functions, limitations in life activity, and grounds for establishing disability, the degree of loss of ability to work, or social protection measures. Referral and examination are regulated by the MSE Rules, in 2026, they were amended, including with respect to certain digital and proactive procedures. A diagnosis of ASD in itself does not automatically mean the establishment of disability.
where_encountered_en: Referral from a medical organization, state service for establishing disability, registration of social support measures.
example_en: The medical organization compiles the necessary information for the MSE, the authorized service reviews it and makes an expert decision in accordance with the established procedure.
dont_confuse_en: A diagnosis of ASD in itself does not equate to disability status. The PMPK primarily determines educational needs, the VKK considers medical grounds, the decision on disability is made by the Medical and Social Expertise Commission.
parent_takeaway_en: Check with your treating physician and the VKK about the basis for the referral and the completion of Form No. 031/u. The procedures for in-person, remote, and proactive assessments vary, the revised Rules of the Medical and Social Expertise Commission contain amendments effective July 12 and August 25, 2026. For your specific situation, check the current version and the available appeal procedure.

definition_en: Early intervention is comprehensive assistance to young children and their families with developmental disabilities or those at risk of developing them. Goals may include communication, movement, play, and participation in everyday activities, as well as parental support. In Kazakhstan, the rules for organizing developmental screening (as amended by the Order of the Ministry of Health dated August 21, 2025, No. 82) provide for an assessment of the development of children from birth to six years of age and, if signs of risk are identified, a consultation with a multidisciplinary team with the development of an individual early intervention program (IEIP) according to established conditions, and, if necessary, referral to the PMPK. Screening, clinical diagnosis, and early intervention are different processes. Actual availability of services is clarified at the location of application.
where_encountered_en: Pediatric appointments, developmental screening, patronage, development and early intervention centers, referrals to specialists.
example_en: The child has been diagnosed with early communication difficulties, the team, together with the family, is identifying ways to support request-making during routine play and caregiving.
dont_confuse_en: Early intervention does not mean waiting for an official diagnosis of ASD and is not the name of a single, mandatory treatment method. There is no promise to "prevent autism" or guarantee the elimination of developmental disabilities.
parent_takeaway_en: If developmental concerns are present, discuss needs with the pediatrician and available early intervention options, even while diagnostic clarification is underway. Find out what goals are included in the program and how the family's support will be measured.

category: Basics, classification, and language about autism
definition_en: Neurodevelopment is the change in the structure and function of the nervous system as a child grows and gains experience. It is associated with the development of perception, movement, attention, language, learning, and self-regulation. The pace of maturation and skill acquisition varies, so specialists consider different areas of development dynamically, rather than making conclusions based on a single child's action.
where_encountered_en: Consultation with a pediatrician, discussion of developmental milestones, neuropsychological or speech therapy report.
example_en: The doctor asks when the child began using gestures, playing with others, and following simple instructions: these are different aspects of neurodevelopment.
dont_confuse_en: Neurodevelopment is a process, not a separate diagnosis. Neurodevelopmental disorder is a diagnostic category, and normal developmental variability in itself is not a pathology.
parent_takeaway_en: If you have questions about development, record observations in several areas and discuss them with your doctor, report separately any loss of previously acquired skills.

category: Basics, classification, and language about autism
definition_en: Neurodivergence is a non-medical descriptive term for characteristics of thinking, attention, perception, or information processing that differ from what is considered typical functioning. The term is used, for example, in relation to autistic people and people with ADHD. Its boundaries depend on the context, as it is not a single diagnostic category.
where_encountered_en: Discussion of inclusion in school, materials about neurodiversity, a person's self-description.
example_en: A teenager says that he or she considers himself or herself neurodivergent and asks to receive instructions in writing.
dont_confuse_en: Neurodivergence does not automatically mean ASD, intellectual disability, or the need for a specific therapy, it is not a substitute for a clinical examination.
parent_takeaway_en: Clarify not only the general label, but also the specific communication styles, sensory preferences, and learning environments that are appropriate for the person.

category: Basics, classification, and language about autism
definition_en: Neurotypicality is a descriptive term typically applied to people whose developmental and information-processing characteristics, in a given context, closely match common expectations. It arose in discussions about neurodiversity and does not have a single clinical test or diagnostic code.
where_encountered_en: Publications about neurodiversity, school discussions, conversations about communication characteristics.
example_en: The text compares the lesson arrangements typical for neurotypical students with those that are more comfortable for some neurodivergent students.
dont_confuse_en: "Neurotypical" does not equate to "healthy in all respects" or "without difficulties," and "neurodivergent" does not mean "worse."
parent_takeaway_en: Use the term only where the comparison truly helps explain needs, rather than dividing children into right and wrong.

category: Basics, classification, and language about autism
definition_en: Diagnostic criteria are an agreed-upon set of features, rules, and clarifying conditions by which a specialist evaluates whether a clinical picture corresponds to a specific diagnosis. When assessing ASD, they take into account the characteristics of social communication and interaction, repetitive or restricted patterns of behavior, the development of manifestations, their impact on life, and alternative explanations.
where_encountered_en: Discussion of the conclusion, DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 criteria, and differential diagnosis.
example_en: The doctor collects information from the family and school and compares the observed picture with the criteria of the diagnostic classification.
dont_confuse_en: Matching several features from the internet does not mean fulfilling all criteria. The screening questionnaire and clinical criteria have different purposes.
parent_takeaway_en: Ask for an explanation of which criteria the specialist considers fulfilled, what remains unclear, and what data the conclusion is based on.

category: Basics, classification, and language about autism
definition_en: ICD-10 is the tenth revision of the World Health Organization's International Classification of Diseases, used to systematize diagnoses and their coding. In ICD-10, autism and some related historical categories are located in group F84 "Pervasive developmental disorders." Specific codes and names may appear in old or current documents, depending on the version of the classification adopted in the country.
where_encountered_en: Medical extracts, certificates, statistical forms, archival reports.
example_en: The old report indicates code F84.0: the specialist explains which diagnostic category they designated in the system used.
dont_confuse_en: ICD-10 and ICD-11 have different structures: you cannot independently replace F84 with 6A02 or interpret the historical name as a new diagnosis.
parent_takeaway_en: If there is a discrepancy between the codes, request clarification from the organization that issued the document, for administrative procedures, the current classification version is important.

category: Basics, classification, and language about autism
definition_en: A diagnostic specifier is an additional characteristic that clarifies the diagnosis already described. For ASD, different classification systems may separately list features of intellectual development, functional language, comorbid conditions, and support needs. The specifier helps to clarify the clinical picture but does not replace the description of daily living skills.
where_encountered_en: A clinical report, discussion of the ICD-11 code or DSM-5-TR criteria.
example_en: The specialist explains why the child's functional language is specified separately in the diagnostic record.
dont_confuse_en: The DSM-5-TR level of support and the ICD-11 specification code cannot be mechanically considered the same. The specifier is not a permanent prognosis for life.
parent_takeaway_en: Ask for each specification to be explained in simple terms and the assessment results underlying it.

category: Basics, classification, and language about autism
definition_en: Diagnostic overshadowing is a clinical error in which new symptoms or difficulties are inappropriately attributed to an existing diagnosis. For example, an autistic person's complaints of pain, anxiety, or insomnia may not be independently assessed if they are attributed to autism. The opposite error can also occur: signs of autism may be mistakenly attributed to another previously identified condition.
where_encountered_en: Medical and psychological consultations, discussion of comorbidities and access to care.
example_en: After a sudden change in a child's sleep, a doctor checks for possible pain, illness, and stress, instead of immediately declaring it "a feature of ASD."
dont_confuse_en: This is the name of a diagnostic error, not another disorder. The presence of autism does not exclude other medical and psychiatric conditions.
parent_takeaway_en: If new symptoms occur, ask to evaluate a specific complaint separately, describing the onset and dynamics of changes.

category: Basics, classification, and language about autism
definition_en: Broader Autism Phenotype (BAP) is a research term for certain social communication characteristics, behavioral flexibility, or thinking style that resemble autistic traits but are insufficient for a clinical diagnosis of ASD. It is also studied in relatives of autistic people, boundaries and measurement methods vary across studies.
where_encountered_en: Research articles on family studies, autism genetics, and psychological characteristics.
example_en: Family studies assess mild communication skills in relatives without diagnosing them with ASD.
dont_confuse_en: BAP is not a diagnosis of "mild autism," does not have a generally accepted self-diagnosis test, and does not necessarily mean that the relative has ASD.
parent_takeaway_en: Do not use the BAP research scale instead of clinical assessment, if real difficulties arise, discuss needs independently of research results.

category: Basics, classification, and language about autism
definition_en: Identity-based language places the definition before the person, for example, "an autistic person", person-first language uses the expression "a person with autism". Both variants are found in professional and public speech. The preferences of autistic people themselves, families, and communities vary and should be taken into account, especially when addressing a specific person.
where_encountered_en: Expert opinions, school website, articles, public discussions, and personal communication.
example_en: A teenager asks to be called "an autistic person", while another prefers "a person with autism" - if possible, both wishes are respected.
dont_confuse_en: One form should not be declared to be the only correct one for all people or use medical terminology to devalue self-identification.
parent_takeaway_en: Whenever possible, ask about the preferred form of address, In materials for a general audience, forms can be carefully alternated without being overbearing.

definition_en: Prosody is the melody and organization of speech: intonation, stress, tempo, rhythm, pauses, pitch and volume. Prosodic features help express meaning, emotion, and phrase structure. When assessing speech, a specialist pays attention to how a person emphasizes words, constructs questions, and changes the rhythm of an utterance.
where_encountered_en: Speech therapy examination, motor speech assessment, description of intonation in diagnostic materials.
example_en: The phrases "You've come" and "Have you arrived?" are pronounced with different intonations, so they sound like a statement and a question.
dont_confuse_en: Atypical prosody in itself does not confirm autism, apraxia of speech, or any one condition, it also depends on the language and speech situation.
parent_takeaway_en: If intonation makes mutual understanding difficult, discuss specific communication situations, and not just the goal of making speech “normal.”

definition_en: Articulation is the formation of speech sounds through the coordinated movements of the tongue, lips, lower jaw, and other speech organs, as well as the work of the airflow and voice. An articulatory assessment examines the precision of individual sounds and their pronunciation in words and connected speech.
where_encountered_en: Speech therapy sessions, pronunciation assessment, and a conclusion about speech difficulties.
example_en: The child has difficulty pronouncing a specific sound, although the order of the other sounds in the word is usually preserved.
dont_confuse_en: Articulatory difficulties do not automatically equate to a language disorder or apraxia of speech. Pronunciation peculiarities when using another native language or dialect are not necessarily an error.
parent_takeaway_en: Ask for clarification on which sounds are causing difficulty and how this affects the intelligibility of speech in real-life communication.

definition_en: Phonological processes are regular ways of changing or simplifying the sound structure of words. During speech acquisition, some such patterns are typical for a certain age and language, persistence, unusualness, or a significant impact on speech intelligibility may require evaluation by a specialist. For example, a difficulty may concern an entire group of sounds or combinations, rather than a single sound.
where_encountered_en: Speech-language pathologist's report, analysis of pronunciation errors and speech development.
example_en: The child systematically simplifies consonant clusters in different words, the speech-language pathologist checks whether this is appropriate for the child's age and language.
dont_confuse_en: A phonological process is not the same as a single articulatory distortion. Not all patterns common to English are the same for Russian and Kazakh.
parent_takeaway_en: Find out what recurring patterns are found, in which languages, and how they affect the child's communication.

definition_en: Dysarthria is a motor speech disorder associated with difficulties in neuromuscular control of movements for breathing, voice production, articulation, and prosody. Speech may become slurred, weak, strained, slow, or less clear, but the manifestations depend on the cause. In children, dysarthria can be associated with various neurological conditions.
where_encountered_en: Examination by a neurologist and speech therapist, motor speech assessment, rehabilitation plan.
example_en: When a child is tired, the clarity of articulation and voice strength decrease, so the specialist evaluates the functioning of different speech systems.
dont_confuse_en: Dysarthria is not synonymous with apraxia of speech: with apraxia, the planning of speech movement programs is paramount, while with dysarthria, their neuromuscular execution is paramount. Both disorders sometimes coexist.
parent_takeaway_en: If a motor speech difficulty is suspected, clarify its nature and the possibility of temporary or permanent use of AAC.

definition_en: Immediate echolalia is the repetition of a sound, word, or phrase immediately after hearing it, or after a short interval. This describes the timing of the repetition, not its meaning: in one case, it may facilitate participation in conversation, in another, it may accompany the processing of what was heard, or serve another function.
where_encountered_en: Speech therapy observation, discussion about speech development, communication characteristics.
example_en: An adult asks, "Do you want water?" and the child immediately repeats, "Do you want water?", the meaning must be determined based on the situation, not guessed.
dont_confuse_en: Immediate echolalia does not automatically mean agreement, lack of understanding, or a specific stage of GLP/NLA. Repetition can have different functions.
parent_takeaway_en: Note what happened before the repetition, how the child responded in other ways, and whether the repetition was directed at the interlocutor.

definition_en: Delayed echolalia is the repetition of a previously heard speech sequence after a significant interval: later in the day, several days later, or in a different situation. The source may be the words of loved ones, cartoons, songs, and other overheard statements. The use of a phrase in a new context may carry personal or communicative meaning.
where_encountered_en: Speech therapy examination, description of speech characteristics, family observations.
example_en: The child says a phrase from a cartoon when he or she wants to end the game, the specialist studies whether it has a specific meaning for the child.
dont_confuse_en: Delayed echolalia does not equal a confirmed diagnosis of GLP, does not prove that the meaning of the phrase is known, and does not in itself require the NLA protocol.
parent_takeaway_en: Write down the exact words and context so that you and your speech therapist can look for a possible function, rather than automatically suppressing repetition.

definition_en: Scripting is the use of memorized sequences of words, prepared lines, or phrases from previous situations, films, and other sources. Scripts can help a person prepare for a conversation, perform a social function, or be a means of self-regulation. The term describes a form of verbal behavior, not a single reason for all repetitions.
where_encountered_en: Conversation with a speech therapist, behavioral observation, discussion of communication characteristics.
example_en: A teenager rehearses in advance how to ask for help at the checkout, a child may use a familiar line from a cartoon in a game.
dont_confuse_en: Scripting overlaps with delayed echolalia, but not every prepared phrase is echolalia, and not every script performs the same function.
parent_takeaway_en: Find out whether a ready-made phrase helps a person express their thoughts, and if necessary, suggest more flexible ways of communication.

definition_en: Non-speaking, or non-verbal, is a descriptive term for someone who does not use verbal communication as their primary means of communication. The reasons for and means of communication vary: the person may understand spoken language, use gestures, writing, symbols, a communicator, or a combination of several methods. The specific means used are best described separately.
where_encountered_en: Speech therapy and AAC assessment, educational plan, discussions about communication accessibility.
example_en: The child does not pronounce words, but confidently selects symbols on a communicator and independently communicates what he or she wants to do.
dont_confuse_en: Lack of verbal communication does not mean a lack of thinking, understanding, intentions, or decision-making ability. The term does not determine intellectual level.
parent_takeaway_en: Find out the person's available ways to communicate requests, refusals, opinions, and questions. Don't require verbal communication before providing AAC.

definition_en: Minimally verbal is a research and practical descriptive term for a person with very limited use of spoken words for independent communication. Numerical thresholds vary across studies: what matters is how functional, varied, and used the words are outside of memorized situations. The term does not automatically describe language comprehension, learning ability, or intelligence.
where_encountered_en: Scientific research, speech therapy reports, discussion of augmentative communication.
example_en: The child uses a few familiar words for requests, but communicates in most situations through gestures and a tablet.
dont_confuse_en: "Minimally verbal" does not mean "understands nothing." There is no single international number of words after which everyone can be assigned this term.
parent_takeaway_en: When assessing, ask to record that the person can communicate independently in all available ways, and not just count the words spoken.

definition_en: Low-tech AAC - communication aids that do not require complex electronics: paper charts with symbols, communication books, alphabet boards, and choice cards. In these, the person chooses a sign, word, or letter to convey a message. AAC without external aids (for example, signing) is also considered a separate category, so not all methods without electronics are strictly classified as low-tech devices.
where_encountered_en: AAC assessment, classroom equipment, speech therapist recommendations, and family training.
example_en: On a walk, a child points to the word "pause" on a laminated board, even if the tablet battery is dead.
dont_confuse_en: Visual schedule cards serve primarily to understand the sequence of events, they do not, by themselves, replace a full-fledged system of independent communication.
parent_takeaway_en: Provide access to tools not only for requests, but also for refusals, comments, questions, and stories, provide a backup option outside the home.

definition_en: High-tech AAC is electronic means of creating and delivering messages using text, symbols, and pre-recorded or synthesized speech. These can be specialized communicators or tablet apps. The method of selecting a message is selected individually: touch, switches, gaze, and other access methods.
where_encountered_en: Speech therapy assessment of AAC, selection of equipment, discussion of accessibility at school.
example_en: The student selects a sequence of symbols using a tablet, and the device reads their message to the class.
dont_confuse_en: Having a tablet does not guarantee full communication: appropriate vocabulary, easy access, partner training, and the right to independently choose the content of the message are all important.
parent_takeaway_en: Choose a system based on the needs and accessibility of the individual, consider charging, portability, vocabulary storage, and a backup communication method in advance.

definition_en: A speech-generating device (SGD) is an electronic AAC device that reproduces a user-selected message verbally, using either speech synthesis or pre-recorded audio phrases. An SGD can be a standalone device or a feature of an app on a tablet. The ability to independently select and create the meaning of a message in an accessible way is important.
where_encountered_en: A speech-language pathologist's opinion on AAC, communicator selection, description of technical support.
example_en: The child selects "I need to rest" on the device, after which a synthesized voice is heard.
dont_confuse_en: An SGD is not evidence of higher or lower intelligence. The computerized voice conveys the user-selected message, it is not the same as host-supported FC/RPM/S2C writing.
parent_takeaway_en: Check the device's usability in different conditions, its individual dictionary, the ability to opt out, and the absence of partner influence on the choice of letters or symbols.

definition_en: AAC core vocabulary is a set of frequently used words and expressions useful in various communication situations: "I," "yet," "not," "want," "help," "where." These words can be combined to request, refuse, ask questions, tell, and comment. In Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC), core vocabulary is supplemented with individual words - names of people, foods, places, and interests.
